feed.description: Software engineering conversations: reliability, architecture, delivery, and the tradeoffs nobody puts in the blog post.
feed.title: Practical Systems

bullets: Reliability is a property of the whole system rather than any single component, meaning failures emerge from interactions, not isolated parts.
The discipline of systems thinking requires managing interactions across components, not just optimizing individual boxes.
Outages are rarely caused by a single failing component—most incidents stem from how components interact unpredictably.
Production risk mirrors portfolio risk: both involve managing unknowns by naming them in advance before they cause failure.
The ability to describe a failure in advance enables designing around it, while unexpected failures are the ones that ultimately cause outages.
Service meshes and financial portfolios are both systems of correlated bets, where the whole is greater than the sum of its parts.
Risk management in production is fundamentally about identifying and naming risks before they materialize.
Reliability and risk are the same question in different clothing—both demand explicit, proactive management of interdependencies.
